commit.subject: fix(site): demo data must pass a privacy gate before it is written or published

entries.text:
A reviewer (GPT-6.1-Sol) checked feat/site and verified the two findings below (everything else passed: ledger.json and screenshots are clean, CSP and injection fine, claims accurate). Fix both on feat/site (new commits, no rebase), each with a check that fails first:
- P1: make publication fail-closed. Add a privacy gate that runs both in make-data.sh (before writing ledger.json) and in `pnpm run site:build` (before embedding): walk every string in the demo data and fail on any absolute path outside /work/wordfreq, any email other than the demo identities, any URL not on a short allowlist, and anything matching values taken from the environment at run time ($HOME, $USER, `git config user.email`/`user.name`, hostname, names of directories under <path>, <path>, <path> and <path>). Print the offending string paths. Put the pure check in a module with a unit test (planted email, foreign path, skill name, allowed demo strings pass).
- P2: remove the personal examples from make-data.sh and the README (no unslop, <project>-age, <private>, or other names from this machine); express those scrubs generically (e.g. drop actions that read files outside the repo; strip npm warn lines) and let the gate catch the rest.
Do NOT start Docker/<product> or regenerate the data unless the gate shows the committed ledger.json is unclean; run the gate on the committed data instead. Same verification and commit rules (no push). Report commits and verification.

Review findings:

── assistant · just now
I would fix the two privacy findings before public release.

- **[P1] The demo generator lets unknown private text pass through.** See `site/demo/make-data.sh:30`, `:43`, and `:85`.
  - It removes one skill path and a fixed list of strings. Other text survives. For example, `Contact alice@example.com` or output from another private skill remains unchanged. The later secret patterns do not remove ordinary emails or skill text. There is no final privacy check before writing `ledger.json`. `scripts/site.ts:45` then checks the data schema and embeds the data without another redaction pass.
  - What I’d do here is allow only approved demo text and paths. Reject unknown strings before replacing `ledger.json`, and repeat that check during the public build. Exact replacements can help, but they cannot be the publication gate.

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
    A[Private rollout] --> B[Fixed replacements]
    B --> C[Secret patterns]
    C --> D[ledger.json]
    D --> E[Schema check]
    E --> F[Public demo]
  ```

- **[P2] The scrub script itself reveals the developer’s setup.** See `site/demo/make-data.sh:30`, `:34`, and `:40`.
  - It names the personal `unslop` skill, identifies `<project>-age` as a setting in the developer’s npm config, and includes the username `<private>`. Removing these from the demo does not remove them from this source file.
  - What I’d do here is remove the personal examples and use neutral input fixtures. This affects publication of the `site/` source. The build does **not** copy this script or README into `site/dist`.

What is fine:

- I found no private identity, home path, email, hostname, token, account setting, or model setting in the committed `ledger.json`. I read its 256 string values. All four WebP screenshots show only demo content.
- The landing page has no scripts or remote resource loads. Its CSP permits only local styles and images. See `site/index.html:7`.
- The demo escapes every `<` in embedded JSON, uses a script hash in its CSP, and renders Markdown images as links. I found no script injection path from the committed data. See `src/core/ledgerSite.ts:67`, `vite.site.config.ts:32`, and `src/web/code.tsx:204`.
- The feature, install, and CI descriptions match the inspected code. The self-hosted section clearly says that nothing is built yet. See `site/index.html:230`.
- A successful `pnpm run site:build` rebuilds the viewer template, removes old output, and reads the committed demo data again. It does not reuse an old demo page. Missing required files cause failure. See `package.json:25` and `scripts/site.ts:32`.

This was a git-only review of the three commits through `c87738c`. I made no changes and ran no builds, tests, containers, browsers, or servers.

I'm figuring out where this privacy-related transform logic should live — weighing whether it belongs in the core browser-safe module or in a site-specific scripts location alongside its test file.

I'm designing a pure `findPrivate` function that scans data against allowed roots, emails, hosts, and forbidden terms, returning flagged matches with their path and reason. Then I need to handle the harder part: gathering environment context like home directory, username, git config, and hostname at the edges, likely through Effect-based file system and process utilities, while making sure `make-data.sh` can also invoke this same privacy check — so I'm sketching out a shared `privacyGate` module that both the site script and shell script can call into.

site.ts gathers env via Effect and runs findPrivate; if invoked with `--check FILE` it only validates that file and exits, which make-data.sh calls before moving the ledger into place. For the privacy rules, I need to walk every string in the data including object keys, tracking paths like `commits[1].entry.entries[3].output`, and detect absolute paths with a regex while allowlisting <private> like `/work/wordfreq`, `/bin/zsh`, and shebang lines such as `/usr/bin/env node`.

I realize the "fail on any absolute path outside /work/wordfreq" rule would break legitimate system paths like `/bin/zsh`, so I need an allowlist covering `/bin/*`, `/usr/bin/*`, `/usr/local/bin/*`, and `/dev/null`. There's also a tricky edge case: JS regex literals like `/^\d+$/` or `/\p{L}.../gu` look like absolute paths syntactically, so my path-detection regex needs to require genuine path-like character segments to avoid false positives on regex literals in the data.

I'm confirming that URLs like "https://x.com/a" won't falsely match the path regex since the lookbehind fails right after the double slash. I'm also considering edge cases like `~/` home-relative paths and deciding they should be excluded too, then moving to designing the email regex to permissively match <private> like demo@example.com or agent@example.

For the email pattern, I realize requiring an alphabetic TLD (like `\.[A-Za-z]{2,}`) prevents false positives on version strings like "wordfreq@1.0.0", since "1.0.0" doesn't end in letters. For URLs, I'm defining a scheme-based regex and considering a small allowlist of safe hosts like example.com, example.org, and localhost to avoid flagging common placeholder domains.

Now I'm thinking through how to detect environment-derived secrets in values — matching against HOME, USER, git identity, hostname, skill names, and project directory names — but worrying that generic words from the <path> directory list (like "docs", "loop", "test") could cause false positives if they coincide with ordinary demo text, so I need word-boundary matching rather than naive substring checks.

I need a cleaner principle rather than guessing word-by-word collisions against demo data. Maybe the rule should be: only flag a skill/directory name if it matches case-sensitively against the actual env value and isn't just a common standalone word also used generically in the text — but that's circular, so I should test candidates directly against the sample data and set thresholds empirically rather than trying to reason it out abstractly.

I should also check other identifying strings: the full HOME path, USER, hostname, and git identity values like user.name and email, all needing whole-word case-insensitive matching. For gathering these in code, I'd rely on Effect's Config module rather than raw process.env, since node:os doesn't appear to have a flagged Effect equivalent while path does.

Now I want to check how the Ledger module runs git commands and how it reads env vars and home directory, so let me look at that helper and the filesystem reading logic.
I'll start with how the server reads the environment and runs git, so the gate's edge code can match.

entries.text:
Only "empty" collides as a dictionary word, so the exemption covers it—but this fails closed on machines without the dictionary available, where English-word directory names would legitimately clash. That seems acceptable as long as the error message explains why, though I'm second-guessing whether "empty" would still break <private> on a typical dev machine with a directory by that name.

The dictionary exemption should only apply to directory names, never to identity values like username or hostname—if someone's hostname happens to be a common word, it should still get flagged. For matching, I want case-insensitive comparison with word-boundary checks so <private> like email addresses and paths match correctly without false positives on substrings.

I should skip very short values (under 3 characters) to avoid noisy matches on <private> like a single-letter skill name. For paths, I need to allow absolute paths under /work/wordfreq plus a small allowlist of legitimate system paths like shell binaries and /usr/bin/env, since the general rule of flagging any absolute path outside the project would otherwise break normal shell invocations.

I also need rules for home-directory paths and word-boundary path segments, plus a check on URL allowlisting and an email regex for approved demo addresses. For output, I'm planning to report the offending match alongside its location path (like commits[1].entry.entries[3].output), printing the matched snippet since this runs locally.

For the module, I'll put the pure logic in scripts/privacy.ts with its own test file, checking whether the test runner picks up scripts/ by default and how other pure-function tests are structured. For the CLI, I'm deciding whether the gate should expose a privacyGate(data) function callable from both make-data.sh and the site build step, using import.meta.main to handle the standalone execution mode.

I want to write the test first so it fails due to the missing module, then confirm the gate actually fails against planted private data before moving to the pass case -- and I need a similar "fails first" check for the second gate, maybe a grep-based verification.

For that second check, I'm considering running the privacy gate directly against the site source files themselves (make-data.sh, README) treating each as raw text, since those scripts contain many absolute paths like temp dirs and binary locations that the path-detection rule would need to handle carefully to avoid false positives.

I think the cleanest approach is to make the gate's rule set configurable per-call — applying only the environment-value/identity rule when scanning source files, and skipping path/URL checks since those legitimately appear in scripts. I'm sketching an interface where rules like `paths` are optional, so callers can selectively enable just the checks relevant to detecting personal names or machine-specific values.

I need to handle the "/" prefix case specially so it matches everything, since appending a slash would break the match. Then I'm second-guessing whether running the gate against current source files will still trip on leftover strings like "<private>" or "unslop" after cleanup, and wondering if npmrc-style keys need to be added to the forbidden list too.

But a bigger issue just occurred to me: the project directory names themselves ("toolreader", "toolreader-demo") appear constantly throughout the README and scripts, so a naive source gate would flag them everywhere. I probably need to exempt the project's own name generically rather than hardcoding exceptions.

I think making DEMO_REPO a required parameter rather than a default removes that machine-specific path from the source entirely. And for ROLLOUTS, instead of a hardcoded date path, I should discover rollouts dynamically by matching session_meta cwd against the demo repo's real path—that's more generic and avoids baking in specifics.

For collision exemptions, I'll exempt dictionary words plus the repo's own name ("toolreader"), then just run the scrubber and iterate on whatever else collides. I also need to generalize the README's description of what's being scrubbed, and apply consistent generic replacements in make-data.sh, like swapping the actual repo path for something like /work/wordfreq.

Beyond that, I need to drop any tool-call items or command executions referencing paths outside the repo root — a generic version of the earlier skill-file removal. I'll write a predicate that checks a serialized payload for absolute paths outside the allowed repo directory and system binaries, and use it to filter out both custom_tool_call inputs and item_completed command executions that read external locations.

I'm reconsidering the $HOME rewrite — maybe simpler to drop it entirely and let the gate catch home paths rather than rewriting them to "~". I should also strip npm warn lines generically across outputs, and consider removing assistant sentences that explicitly name a skill, keeping the rule generic rather than specific to this case.

Separately, I'm thinking about replacing $USER occurrences with "dev" while preserving alignment/padding so columns don't shift, since I can't regenerate the full dataset end-to-end without Docker and will need to validate just the Python scrubbing logic against existing samples.

Without Docker, I can still copy rollouts into /tmp and run the scrub portion directly to verify: no leftover SKILL.md references, no npm warnings, no "<private> staff"-style entries, the skill sentence removed, and that the set of kept item ids matches the previous scrub exactly. To make this testable in isolation, I'm considering pulling the Python scrubbing logic out into its own file like site/demo/scrub.py rather than keeping it inline in make-data.sh.

I'm also sketching the privacy gate flow: after extracting ledger.json into a temp file, run the privacyGate script against it on the host before moving it to the output location, so it uses host environment values. In site.ts, I need to call the gate on a range before embedding, which means wiring up an Effect that gathers config, reads the directory via FileSystem, and spawns a child process using the Node services layer.

Now I'm designing privacyGate.ts itself — defining functions to collect machine-specific values like identities and hostnames, build privacy rules from them, and run a gate that scans a labeled value for findings and fails with a listed message if anything private is detected, plus a CLI entry point that accepts file paths and a `--source` flag for source-text-specific rules. I'm also considering reading the system dictionary file if it exists to help flag plain English words versus private data.

I should exempt dictionary words case-insensitively when scanning, and think through whether the repo's own directory name ("toolreader") should be exempt in source mode versus data mode — data shouldn't reference it, but source mode legitimately does, and I need to check whether the demo repo name or README text would trip the gate. I'll look at existing core tests to match their style before finalizing this.



Only "empty" turns out to be a common dictionary word colliding with the demo text, so I'll have the gate check `$HOME`, `$USER`, git identity, and hostname as-is while skipping directory names that are ordinary English words. Next I'll check test conventions and Node's `import.meta.main` types.

I'm defining a tagged error for privacy gate failures that carries the list of findings, with the runner logging each as an error and failing the process, then checking whether there's any OS module usage I need to worry about flagging.



Tests initially failed due to the missing module, but all 6 now pass once it's added. Next I'll build the Effect edge in `scripts/privacyGate.ts`, which gathers machine-level values at runtime and is used both as a CLI by `make-data.sh` and as an import in `site.ts`.

entries.text: I'm checking that decodeRange preserves unknown fields correctly, which looks fine. Now I want to make a minimal edit to make-data.sh so the final python step writes to a temp ledger file, runs the node gate, then copies the result over—saving the bigger structural changes for the next commit. Let me look at the tail of that script first.
Now the gate in `make-data.sh`, before it writes `ledger.json`:

entries.text:
Good, `set -e` ensures the gate stops on failure. I want to verify this by temporarily swapping in the planted ledger data, confirming site:build fails and site/dist stays untouched, then restoring the original and confirming the normal build passes along with check/typecheck/test.



I'll temporarily swap in bad data for ledger.json and run the build to confirm it fails closed without touching site/dist, then restore the original file from git and rerun a clean build.

entries.text:
I should also verify it catches machine-specific values like a planted "unslop" skill directory name or the $USER value — I'll add a couple of test strings via Python and run the gate CLI to confirm. Then I'll check, typecheck, and test before committing the P1 changes, keeping make-data.sh limited to just the gate lines for now since the P2 changes come later.



Confirmed `site:build` fails and leaves `site/dist` untouched when data is corrupted, then builds cleanly after restoring. Next I'll run one more check using live machine-specific values—`$USER`, a skill directory name, and the git name—pulled at runtime rather than hardcoded.

entries.title: python3 - $USER $SKILL "$(git config user.name)" <<E · node scripts/privacyGate.ts <path> 2>&1
entries.command:
cd . && SKILL=$(ls <path> | grep -v -x -F -f <(tr A-Z a-z </usr/share/dict/words) | head -1) && python3 - "$USER" "$SKILL" "$(git config user.name)" <<'E'
import json,sys
d=json.load(open('site/demo/ledger.json'))
e=d['commits'][1]['entry']['entries']
e[1]['text'] += f" Ran by {sys.argv[1]} with the {sys.argv[2]} skill, as {sys.argv[3]}."
json.dump(d,open('<path>','w'))
E
node scripts/privacyGate.ts <path> 2>&1 | grep -v -e Experimental -e '^\s*at ' | sed "s/\"[^\"]*\"\$/\"<value>\"/" | tail -4; echo "(values masked here)"

fix(site): demo data must pass a privacy gate before it is written or published

scripts/privacy.ts checks every string, object keys included, and allows only what it knows:
absolute paths under /work/wordfreq (plus the shell and env binaries), the two demo emails and
example.com URLs. It also rejects this machine's own values, read at run time: home, user, git
identity, hostname, and the names of local skills and projects. make-data.sh runs the gate before
replacing ledger.json, and `pnpm run site:build` before building anything. Both print the path of
every string they reject.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
